title: Bring one handover to a consulting conversation
content:
You do not need technical language to explain useful work. Bring one task that loses information, takes repeated entry or needs too much chasing.

A one-page starting brief

  1. What starts the task?
  2. Which tools and roles touch it?
  3. Where does it wait, repeat or become unclear?
  4. What should a useful result look like?
  5. Which decision should stay with a person?
  6. What happens when the information is missing or unusual?

Use a fictional example to explain the shape of the process. Do not send passwords, customer records, employee details or private documents through a discovery tool.

Understand the next step

Renzo personally replies to enquiries and designs and builds the agreed work. If a scoped workflow review is useful, its fee and deliverables are agreed before starting. A build is separately scoped. An enquiry does not subscribe you to marketing, book a meeting automatically or commit you to paid work.

Explore a relevant example, then send your process, tools and desired result. The purpose is a useful business conversation, not a technology test.

title: When a running automation should pause
content:
A process that usually works still needs a clear response to a missing record, changed permission or failed connection. The useful question is what should stop, who should know and how work can resume.

Name the stop condition

For one running process, identify the event that would make its next action unsafe or unreliable. Examples include a duplicate invoice, an unmatched reference or a required approval that has not happened. Those are conditions to handle, not evidence that your process has already failed.

Name the owner and recovery

Who sees the exception? What should they check? Which work can continue? After correction, should the process retry the same action or begin again? Keep a record that helps avoid creating the same transaction twice.

Use fictional records to test both the normal path and the pause. A success-only demonstration cannot explain recovery. The safeguards explorer shows a duplicate invoice stopping and unresolved reporting being reviewed and rerun.

For an existing process, tell Renzo its trigger, tools and failure you need to handle. A paid review or improvement is scoped before work begins.

title: The enquiry was received. Who is following it up?
content:
A customer can receive a quick receipt while their request still waits. To understand the gap, check the next owned action rather than counting automatic replies.

Follow one fictional enquiry

The message arrives. Someone or something identifies its destination. A named person receives enough context to act. If the request is unclear or that person is unavailable, an exception has its own owner and next action.

Write down when the request arrived, when an owner accepted it and what happened next. Keep those moments separate from any acknowledgement timestamp. Use the distinction to decide what the team needs to improve; do not invent a universal response target.

Check the uncertain route

Try a lead outside the usual territory, an existing customer or a team with no capacity. A routing rule should explain the outcome, and a person should be able to review an unusual handover.

The lead-routing demonstration uses fictional records. If your team keeps asking who owns a request, describe the intake, tools and follow-up you want. Renzo replies personally and agrees fees and scope before a paid engagement.

title: Human approval is a feature, not a failure
content:
The point of a better workflow is not to remove people. It is to remove avoidable effort and make important decisions clearer.

Keep people where judgement matters

Approval is valuable when the amount is unusual, the customer relationship is sensitive, the information is incomplete or the decision has a real consequence. Make the review point visible, timely and informed.

Do not make people check everything

Routine cases can move with rules. A good workflow highlights the small number of cases that need attention: missing documents, mismatched values, unclear requests or an exception to policy. This protects judgement from being buried under administration.

Give the reviewer context

A useful approval asks one clear question and shows the source, relevant history and recommended next step. It should not force someone to open five systems just to understand what they are approving.

Design an exit path

Every automated action needs a way to pause, correct and continue. A visible exception queue and clear owner are more trustworthy than an opaque “set and forget” process.

See approval in a job-to-invoice example

The invoice workflow lets a person review unapproved variations before an invoice draft is prepared. This fictional demonstration does not send an invoice or make a payment.

title: Two tools disagree about a customer. Which record wins?
content:
A customer changes a detail in one place. Another tool still holds the old value. Before connecting them, agree how the business will decide which record to trust.

Choose a field and a direction

Start with one practical field: contact email, account reference or service address. Name the system that owns that field and the person responsible for a correction. Decide whether a connection should copy the value, propose a change or flag a difference.

Do not assume the newest timestamp is always right. A recent import may contain an old value. A person may have deliberately corrected the destination. Those cases need an explicit rule or review.

Try one conflict

Use a fictional customer in your worksheet. Write the two values, where they came from and the event that should resolve the conflict. Also write what happens while the difference remains unresolved.

This is a focused ownership exercise. Renzo's consulting site provides the broader systems-connection guide. For your specific conflict, describe the field, tools and review owner. Do not submit customer records or credentials. Renzo agrees scope and fees before paid work.

title: Give each step a job: record, rule, draft or decision
content:
Take one short process and put a label beside each step. This gives you a practical way to discuss AI and automation without needing to choose a product first.

Use four labels

Record: the place the official information belongs. Rule: repeatable work with an agreed instruction. Draft: interpretation or preparation that may need checking. Decision: a person takes responsibility for the consequence.

In Renzo’s confirmed enquiry logic, the message arrives in Outlook. The customer database holds known customer information. AI checks for a match and, when needed, researches the company from its email domain before preparing the brief and meeting reply. Staff approval comes before Zapier sends the reply. The customer confirming a time is a separate event; connected confirmation, calendar/invitation, assignment and CRM updates follow it. Demonstration records are fictional.

Look for the unclear label

If a step does not fit, ask what it needs to know and who owns the result. A process with an unclear decision should not become less visible when software is added.

title: Which number is right? A reporting handover checklist
content:
Before choosing a new dashboard, ask two people to explain the same number. If they give different sources, periods or definitions, the first job is to agree the handover.

Try this with one report

Choose a figure people question in a regular meeting. It might be open enquiries, completed work, available capacity or invoiced revenue. This is a working checklist, not a claim about your reporting time or data quality.

  1. Definition: What does the number include and exclude? Write the unit and the decision it supports.
  2. Period and cut-off: Which dates are included, in which time zone, and when do adjustments stop?
  3. Source and owner: Which record is authoritative? Who can explain a correction?
  4. Freshness: When was each source refreshed? Show missing or stale extracts instead of treating them as zero.
  5. Reconciliation: Which references and totals must agree? Keep a difference separate until it has been resolved.
  6. Exception: Who owns an unresolved difference, when is it reviewed and what can the team decide while it remains open?

A fictional handover

One team counts completed jobs. Another counts invoices issued. Those are different measures, even if both are called “finished work”. Agree the labels before connecting the sources. A daily refresh cannot repair an undefined number.

See a report held for review

The daily reporting story explains how Excel, Xero and Simpro records are matched and reconciled. An unresolved record is held for review and rerun. The demonstration uses fictional records, not business results.

Bring a useful starting point

Write down the report, the disputed measure, its sources and the person who owns the next decision. Do not include private records when experimenting with an AI tool.

title: Why are we entering this twice?
content:
Duplicate entry is not a people problem. It is usually a handover problem.

A job is created in one system, copied into a spreadsheet, then typed into finance software. Each person is trying to keep the business moving. The work is real; the retyping is often unnecessary.

Start with one piece of information

Pick something that gets entered repeatedly: a customer name, job number, invoice amount, new-starter details or a lead. Write down where it starts, who copies it, and where it must end up. This reveals the process between the software—not just the software itself.

Ask four useful questions

  1. Which system should own the record?
  2. Is the next step a repeatable rule or a judgement call?
  3. What must be checked before it moves?
  4. What happens when the information is missing or unusual?

If a step is repeatable, automation can carry it. If information needs interpreting, AI may assist with a draft or classification. If the consequence matters, a person should approve the exception.

Do not automate a bad handover

Connecting two messy processes can make errors move faster. First agree on the source of truth, the minimum information required and the visible exception path. Then connect the routine work.

See the pattern

Explore the job-to-invoice workflow to see an illustrative example: the system moves known information, an automation applies consistent steps, and a person keeps review and sending decisions.

A better first measure

Count duplicate entries and waiting points for one week. That gives you a credible starting point—without pretending every improvement can be reduced to a dollar figure.
